newsitem.title: USA: Pentagon reviewing alleged harassment of gays.
newsitem.headline: Pentagon reviewing alleged harassment of gays.

text.p: The Pentagon confirmed on Wednesday it had begun a formal review of allegations that military investigators were wrongfully conducting aggressive inquiries into the sex lives of gay service members.
Defence Department spokesman Jim Turner confirmed a report in Wednesday's Washington Post that the step was taken after a Pentagon meeting on Monday.

Other Defence officials, who asked not to be identified, stressed that the review was not aimed at changing the 3-year-old Pentagon policy on homosexuals in uniform but to make sure the controversial plan was enforced fairly.

Gay rights advocates charged earlier this year that military commanders had turned a blind eye to the harassment, which would violate rules negotiated with military leaders and Congress during President Bill Clinton's early months in office.
Under the policy dubbed "don't ask, don't tell," the military agreed to stop searching out gays provided they kept their sexual orientation private.
Being homosexual is no longer a bar to service in the U.S. military, but admitting homosexuality or engaging in homosexual acts can result in expulsion from the service.
Since the regulation took effect in early 1994, the number of gays dismissed from military service has climbed 42 percent, reaching 850 in 1996, the Post reported.

Based on preliminary analysis, officials told the Post that some homosexual cases had been mishandled, but they called the errors little more than minor technical violations and attributed them largely to inadvertence or unfamiliarity with the policy's complexities.
